title: Psalm 151
subtitle: the youngest son, a harp, a sword, and the shame lifted
lead: Psalm 151 is seven short verses in David's voice. He was small among his brothers and kept his father's sheep; his hands made an instrument and his fingers tuned a harp (1:1–2). God sent his messenger, took him from the sheep and anointed him, though his brothers were good-looking and big (1:4–5). He went out against the Philistine, who cursed him by his idols, drew the giant's sword, cut off his head and lifted the shame from Israel (1:6–7). In the Greek Psalter it follows Psalm 150 under a heading that calls it David's own, "in his own hand," but "outside the count." A longer Hebrew form in two poems was found in the Psalms Scroll from Qumran Cave 11 (11Q5), and the two can now be read side by side.

Who reads it as Scripture. The Orthodox churches print it in their Psalters after Psalm 150, keeping the heading's "outside the number," and the Coptic Orthodox Church reads it each year on Bright Saturday (the day before the Resurrection feast). It is not in the Jewish Bible, whose Psalter has 150 psalms, and the Council of Trent defined "the Davidical Psalter, consisting of a hundred and fifty psalms." It is not among the Apocrypha of Article VI or the KJV. Catholic and Protestant churches do not count it as Scripture, though Latin Vulgate Psalters carried it "outside the number."
facts: Printed in Orthodox Psalters after Psalm 150, "not numbered with the one hundred and fifty psalms" (Asser's Orthodox Psalter, 2005); read by the Coptic Orthodox Church on Bright Saturday (the day before the Resurrection feast) (St-Takla.org). Not in the Catholic canon (Trent: "a hundred and fifty psalms"), not in the KJV Apocrypha or Article VI, not in the Jewish Bible.
The heading says David wrote it "in his own hand." Its author is unknown; the Hebrew form survives first in a scroll from Qumran.

Not known. The Qumran Psalms Scroll (11Q5), which holds the Hebrew, was copied in the first century AD, about AD 30–50 (Wikipedia, "Great Psalms Scroll," which cites Schiffman and Flint); the scroll shows the psalm existed by then, not how much earlier it was composed. The Greek is copied in the great Greek codices of the 300s–400s AD.
Bethlehem and the sheepfold (1 Samuel 16), then the duel with Goliath (1 Samuel 17).

Disputed over time. Scholars long held that it was composed in Greek; since 11Q5 turned up with two Hebrew poems (151A and 151B), Sanders, the scroll's first editor, called the Greek "made from a truncated amalgamation of the two Hebrew psalms," a view Wikipedia's "Psalm 151" says scholars now accept. The Hebrew of 151B survives only briefly, so the Greek's later verses cannot be checked against it.

Greek: Codex Vaticanus (Swete's base text), Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Alexandrinus, the Verona Psalter (R, 500s AD, where a later hand added it) and the Zurich Psalter (T, 600s AD). Hebrew: the Psalms Scroll 11Q5, in the column the ETCBC transcription numbers 28, lines 3–14. Later versions in Syriac, Ethiopic, Armenian and Arabic (St-Takla.org).
A psalm of praise and thanksgiving telling David's own story in the first person.
1 chapter: a heading (1:0) and 7 verses. Brenton's English begins verse 1 with the heading, so his 1:1 is this page's 1:0 and 1:1.
authorship: The heading gives it to David, written in his own hand, and Orthodox Psalters print it as David's, "outside the number."

A later poet's psalm in David's voice, built on 1 Samuel 16–17. Before 11Q5, scholars held that it was composed in Greek; Sanders, the scroll's first editor, held the Greek to be a joined and shortened form of the two Hebrew poems (Wikipedia, "Psalm 151").

The Psalms Scroll places the psalm just after a prose note crediting David with 4,050 psalms and songs composed "through prophecy" given him "from before the Most High." What the scroll was is debated: Sanders held it reflects an arrangement from before the Masoretic Psalter of 150 was fixed; Goshen-Gottstein and Skehan took it for a secondary liturgical collection based on the standard Psalter; Flint proposed a collection of 52 psalms matching the 52 weeks of the solar calendar (Wikipedia, "Great Psalms Scroll").

audience.to: The community whose library held the Qumran Psalms Scroll, which carries it, and then Greek-speaking Jews and Christians who read the Greek Psalter, where the psalm closes the book after Psalm 150. Today it is read by Orthodox Christians in their Psalters and by Coptic Orthodox Christians on Bright Saturday (the day before the Resurrection feast).
audience.why: To praise God for choosing the least likely: the youngest, a shepherd and musician, over his tall, handsome brothers, and then for giving him victory over the giant who mocked Israel. It puts the lesson of 1 Samuel 16:7, that the LORD sees the heart, in David's own voice. Placed at the end of the Psalter, it closes the book of David's songs with the story of how David himself began.
views: At Qumran it stood near the end of a scroll that gathered psalms and other Davidic writings; scholars debate what the scroll was: a variant edition of the Psalter (Sanders) or a liturgical collection based on the standard Psalter (Goshen-Gottstein, Skehan).
A closing psalm for the Greek Psalter
In the Greek Psalter it is an appendix to the 150, a psalm about David that ends the book of David's psalms.

lenses.name: Orthodox
lenses.desc: Orthodox Psalters print the psalm after Psalm 150 with its heading, "not numbered with the one hundred and fifty psalms"; the lens reads it as the Psalter's closing song of David, and notes the Coptic Orthodox use on Bright Saturday (the day before the Resurrection feast).

lenses.name: Historical-critical
lenses.desc: Scholars read it as a poem built on 1 Samuel 16–17, whose Hebrew form in two poems survives in the Qumran Psalms Scroll (11Q5) and may explain the obscure Greek.

lenses.name: Jewish reception
lenses.desc: Not in the Jewish Bible, but its Hebrew stands among the Davidic compositions of a Psalms Scroll from Qumran, with a prose note crediting David with 4,050 songs: scholars differ on what that scroll was: a variant edition of the Psalter (Sanders) or a liturgical collection based on the standard Psalter (Goshen-Gottstein, Skehan) (Wikipedia, "Great Psalms Scroll").

lenses.name: New Testament background
lenses.desc: David the shepherd anointed among his brothers is the background of the shepherd and Son of David themes in the Gospels (Luke 2:8–11; John 10:11); the links are echoes of the larger story, not quotations.

lenses.name: Western churches: read, not Scripture
lenses.desc: Catholic and Protestant readers count 150 psalms (the Council of Trent; the Hebrew Psalter); the psalm is not even among the KJV Apocrypha, and is read as a witness to how David's story was sung.

sections.b: Read 1 Samuel 16–17 first, then the psalm, then the Hebrew of 11Q5 in the variants. The psalm says nothing 1 Samuel does not, except that it calls God's messenger an "angel" (1:4), but it says it as David's own praise. Read it last of all the psalms, as the Greek Psalter places it: after 150 songs of David, a song about David.

The Greek psalm has seven verses. The Hebrew in 11Q5 has two poems: the first (151A) tells of David's youth, his music, God's hearing and his anointing by Samuel, and ends with David made "leader of his people"; the second (151B) begins a story of his first mighty deed and breaks off as he sees the Philistine taunting Israel. On Sanders's view the Greek is made from the two Hebrew poems joined and shortened (Wikipedia, "Psalm 151"). The second poem survives in the scroll for only about two lines, so the Greek's verses 6–7 cannot be compared with it. The strange 1:3 can be read beside the Hebrew (see the note there).

The Plain English Translation is made from the Greek of Swete's Old Testament in Greek, which prints Codex Vaticanus, compared with Brenton's English (1851) and with the readings of Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus and the Verona and Zurich Psalters in Swete's notes. It follows Swete's text in every verse. The Hebrew of 11Q5 is translated in the variants from the Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcription; words the transcription marks as restored are not treated as the scroll's reading. Brenton's verse 1 begins with the heading, so his 1:1 is this page's 1:0 and 1:1.

spec.title: Claude's theory: the Psalter's last word is its first singer
spec.body: The Greek Psalter ends Psalm 150 with "Let every breathing thing praise Yah!" (Psalm 150:6) and then, outside the count, gives David's own story: the small boy whose hands made the first instruments of the Psalter's music. Claude suggests the psalm was placed there on purpose, to close a book of songs with the call of the one who began them, much as the prose note in 11Q5 stands just before it.

prompts: The shepherd boy and his harp (1:1–2)

On a rocky hillside near Bethlehem at dusk, a small red-haired shepherd boy sits among a few sheep, carving and stringing a small wooden harp with his fingers, a reed pipe beside him on the stone; far off, his tall older brothers walk toward a village with their father.

Style: sketched by hand onto an old rolled parchment scroll. Sepia and iron-gall ink linework with charcoal shading, red-ochre and yellow-ochre pigment like Lascaux cave paintings, Egyptian hieroglyphic register lines and small glyph borders, plus a few bold flat shapes of lapis blue in the manner of modern paper cut-outs. Visible parchment grain, uneven hand-drawn lines, soft torn irregular edges that fade into the parchment. No frame, no rectangular border, no sharp corners, no lettering. Wide horizontal composition, 3:2.

reading: The story the psalm retells: the anointing among the brothers, the lyre, Goliath.
The Hebrew form of the psalm and the prose note on David's 4,050 songs.

views: In the Psalter, but outside the count: Orthodox Psalters print it after Psalm 150 with the heading that says it "is not numbered with the one hundred and fifty psalms" (Asser's Psalter, 2005), and an Orthodox parish's answer to a reader says it "has never been considered part of the body of the Psalms themselves."

Read in worship by the Coptic Orthodox Church: "The Coptic Orthodox Church reads that Psalm on the Bright Saturday each year (the day before the Resurrection feast)," says the Coptic church site St-Takla.org.

Not counted among the Psalter's numbered psalms. The Council of Trent defined "the Davidical Psalter, consisting of a hundred and fifty psalms," and Wikipedia's "Psalm 151" says the Catholic Church considers the psalm noncanonical. Latin Psalters carried it all the same: the Vulgate text on CCEL has a Psalm 151 headed "hic psalmus proprie scriptus David et extra numerum cum pugnavit cum Goliad," beginning "pusillus eram inter fratres meos."
No. Article VI's list of books read "for example of life" does not include it, and the KJV Apocrypha does not print it.

No. The Westminster Confession (1.3) says the books commonly called Apocrypha, "not being of divine inspiration, are no part of the canon of the Scripture"; it does not name Psalm 151, which is not among the Hebrew Psalter's 150.

canon.summary: Psalm 151 is printed in Orthodox Psalters after Psalm 150, "outside the number," and read by the Coptic Orthodox Church on Bright Saturday (the day before the Resurrection feast). It is not in the Jewish Bible or the Catholic and Protestant Bibles, which count 150 psalms, and not even in the KJV Apocrypha.
accepted_by: Printed in the Psalter after Psalm 150, with the heading that it "is not numbered with the one hundred and fifty psalms" (Asser's Psalter, after the use of the Orthodox Church, 2005). An Orthodox parish answer says it "has never been considered part of the body of the Psalms themselves."
Read in worship every year on Bright Saturday, the day before the feast of the Resurrection (St-Takla.org, a Coptic Orthodox site, which also names Syriac, Ethiopic, Armenian and Arabic versions).
It survives in some manuscripts of the Syriac Peshitta, and William Wright published a translation of the Syriac version in 1887 (Wikipedia, "Psalm 151").

Considered noncanonical (Wikipedia, "Psalm 151"). The Council of Trent (1546) defined "the Davidical Psalter, consisting of a hundred and fifty psalms," a count that leaves the psalm out; Latin Psalters carried it "outside the number" (the Vulgate text on CCEL, headed "extra numerum"), and the same article says it appears in some Vulgate editions and as a Latin Matins responsory.

Not Scripture, and not among the Apocrypha: it is not in Article VI's list or in the KJV Apocrypha. The Westminster Confession (1.3) says the books commonly called Apocrypha "are no part of the canon of the Scripture" and does not name Psalm 151.

Scholars long held that it never existed in Hebrew; the Hebrew came to light in the Psalms Scroll from Qumran (11Q5), found in 1956. The Jewish Psalter has 150 psalms, and the Wikipedia article on Psalm 151 says most forms of Judaism count the psalm as apocryphal.

provenance.b: The Psalms Scroll from Qumran Cave 11 (11Q5) has two Hebrew poems that match the Greek psalm, in the column the Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcription numbers 28, lines 3–14. The first is headed "Hallelujah. Of David son of Jesse," the second "The beginning of David's mighty deeds after the prophet of God had anointed him." Just before them stands a prose list of David's 4,050 songs. The Hebrew is longer than the Greek; Sanders, the scroll's first editor, held the Greek to be a shortened joining of the two poems (Wikipedia, "Psalm 151").

The great Greek codices copy it after Psalm 150: Swete prints Codex Vaticanus, and his notes give Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus and the Verona and Zurich Psalters. Swete's Introduction says the Psalter of Alexandrinus contains it, and that in the Verona Psalter a later hand added it. Sinaiticus closes with "151 psalms of David"; Alexandrinus counts 150 and the extra psalm (Swete's notes).

A Coptic Orthodox site lists Syriac, Ethiopic, Armenian and Arabic versions. Wikipedia's "Psalm 151" adds that the Syriac survives in some Peshitta manuscripts, which William Wright published in translation in 1887.

rejected_why.h: Outside the number by its own heading
rejected_why.b: The psalm's heading says it is "outside the count." The Orthodox Psalter opened for this page keeps that label, though Codex Sinaiticus counts it as the 151st.

Judaism and the Protestant churches follow the Hebrew Bible's 150 psalms. The Council of Trent also defined a Psalter of 150 psalms. The Hebrew psalm from Qumran shows the poem is old, but not that it was ever part of the Psalter that became the Jewish Bible's.

cited_in.b: The psalm retells the anointing among the brothers. It depends on 1 Samuel, not the reverse; no book of the 66 quotes the psalm.
The duel with Goliath, the curse "by his gods," the beheading with his own sword: the psalm's source.

"Who teaches my hands to fight a war, my fingers to do battle," in a psalm the Greek titles "against Goliath"; Psalm 151's hands and fingers make music. A likely echo between the two Goliath psalms of the Greek Psalter, not a quotation.

reliability.verdict: This is Claude's analysis, not a church's judgment. As a witness to how David's story was told in Hebrew by the first century AD, the psalm is valuable: its Hebrew is in a Qumran scroll copied about AD 30–50. As a text, the Greek is a short and sometimes unclear translation, and the Hebrew is broken off at the end. As history, it adds nothing to 1 Samuel except the word "angel." As teaching, it agrees with 1 Samuel throughout.

sections.b: The Hebrew in 11Q5, with the prose note before it, shows that the scroll's makers credited David with 4,050 compositions written "through prophecy"; whether the scroll was a variant Psalter or a collection for worship is debated (Wikipedia, "Great Psalms Scroll").

The Greek manuscripts agree closely; their differences are small (1:3 "listens" or "will hear me"; 1:4 "oil" or "mercy"). The Hebrew is longer and partly restored at the break in 151B. On Sanders's view the Greek shortened Hebrew poems like these, which would explain why 1:3 is hard.

sections.h: Its claim to be David's own
sections.b: The heading claims David's hand. Nothing outside the heading supports it, and the psalm reads as a retelling of 1 Samuel. The churches that print it keep it "outside the number."

It agrees with 1 Samuel 16–17 on every point but one: it calls the one God sent "his angel," where 1 Samuel has the prophet Samuel, and the Hebrew psalm agrees with 1 Samuel. The Greek word can mean a human messenger, so the difference may be only in English.

how_to_read.b: Read 1 Samuel 16:1–13 and 1 Samuel 17:4–51 beside it, and see how much of the story seven verses can hold.
Read the Hebrew in the variants: the longer Hebrew can help with the shorter Greek.

how_to_read.h: As the end of the Psalter
how_to_read.b: Read it after Psalm 150, as the Greek Psalter does: a song about the singer.
